candidateRows: Whatever else is claimed about Jesus of Nazareth, he certainly existed as a person in history.
This explicitly states the historical-Jesus side's answer to the debate motion and announces the positive case that the remainder of the presentation develops.
After explaining the significance of the issue, Ehrman gives a synopsis of his position and says he will present several strong positive arguments for Jesus's existence.
The alleged nonexistence of ancient Nazareth does not support the conclusion that Jesus never existed.
It removes a stated route from a disputed birthplace premise to Jesus's nonexistence by invoking archaeology and distinguishing birthplace from personal existence.
The mythicist contention that Jesus could not have existed because ancient Nazareth did not exist.
Ehrman says archaeological work identifies first-century remains at Nazareth and adds that even a false birthplace tradition would not establish that its subject was nonexistent.
Stories patterned after myths and traditional narrative types can accumulate around people who nevertheless existed.
The move challenges a major inference from literary or mythic patterning to nonexistence, separating legendary narrative development from the historicity of its subject.
The mythicist inference that gospel parallels to older myths or scriptural patterns show Jesus did not exist.
Ehrman invokes legendary accounts of known figures, especially Caesar Augustus, to argue that stereotyped divine-savior stories do not determine whether their subjects existed.
Multiple independent first-century sources, including traditions rooted in Aramaic Palestine, attest Jesus unusually well.
This supplies a principal positive historical case by arguing for numerous independent traditions, some traceable geographically and linguistically to early Palestinian settings.
Ehrman compares Jesus with other first-century Palestinian Jews, distinguishes sources underlying the canonical gospels, and traces some traditions to early Aramaic-speaking Palestine.
Paul's authentic letters provide early testimony that Jesus was an earthly Jewish teacher crucified by earthly opponents.
The argument places Paul's knowledge close to the traditional death date and treats Paul as an early independent source for a terrestrial rather than purely celestial Jesus.
Ehrman dates Paul's conversion and prior persecution near the traditional crucifixion date, then contrasts Paul's historical Jewish Jesus with a figure killed by demons in space.
Paul's failure to mention many gospel episodes does not show that Paul lacked knowledge of a historical Jesus.
This defends the probative use of Paul against an argument from silence by relating the contents of occasional letters to their limited purposes and circumstances.
The objection that Paul would have mentioned more episodes from Jesus's life if he knew of a historical Jesus.
Ehrman compares Paul's letters with religious letters from his mother and argues that correspondence addressing particular congregational problems need not recount familiar biographical episodes.
Paul personally knew Jesus's brother James and his close disciple Peter, supporting Jesus's historical existence.
The move connects Paul with two people presented as close earthly associates of Jesus and argues that the specific contrast makes biological kinship the relevant meaning.
Ehrman cites Paul's Jerusalem visit, argues that James is distinguished as the Lord's actual brother, compares related Pauline usage, and joins James with Peter as direct associates.
Paul's description of Jesus as crucified refers to an ordinary Roman execution on earth, not a killing in outer space.
This directly contests a celestial interpretation of Paul's Jesus by grounding crucifixion language in the consistently terrestrial Roman penal practice of the period.
The mythicist interpretation that Paul's Jesus was killed by demonic powers in a celestial or outer-space realm.
Ehrman argues that ancient references to crucifixion concern Roman public torture and execution, so Paul's language naturally describes an earthly death inflicted on a criminal.
A crucified Messiah was too contrary to Jewish messianic expectations to be a plausible Christian invention.
The argument treats the embarrassing contradiction between victorious messianic expectations and crucifixion as best explained by followers confronting an actual execution.
The mythicist position that Christians invented Jesus and his identity as a crucified Jewish Messiah.
Ehrman contrasts powerful Jewish messianic expectations with execution as a criminal and argues that Christians proclaimed a crucified Messiah because the man they followed was crucified.
Claims that Jesus's nonexistence had no ancient precedent overlook ancient accusations that Christians fabricated their savior traditions.
This challenges an asserted historical consensus premise by presenting several ancient passages as possible accusations that Christians constructed Christ or devised myths about him.
Ehrman's claim that Jesus mythicism is modern and that even ancient opponents assumed Jesus had existed.
Price interprets passages associated with Justin Martyr, Celsus, and Second Peter as indicating that fabrication or mythmaking accusations against Christianity existed in antiquity.
Dating traditions to shortly after Jesus's supposed crucifixion presupposes the Gospel chronology whose historicity is disputed.
The argument challenges whether claims of very early tradition can independently establish Jesus when their chronological framework already assumes the disputed narrative.
Ehrman's claim that traditions about Jesus can be traced to within a few years of his crucifixion.
Price argues that without a historical Jesus there is no independently fixed starting point, so descriptions of Peter as Jesus's companion merely assume the narrative at issue.
Removing miraculous content does not reveal a plausible remembered historical core, but leaves banal incidents with no reason to be preserved.
This directly attacks the historical-Jesus reconstruction method by denying that legendary narratives can be reduced to an independently credible ordinary preacher.
Ehrman's position that legendary shaping can coexist with a historical event or person beneath the legends.

Price compares a demythologized Jesus to Clark Kent without Superman, offers deliberately mundane versions of miracle stories, and argues such incidents would neither survive nor generate Christianity.
Pliny, Tacitus, and early oral Gospel traditions provide multiple attestations of Christian hearsay rather than independent evidence for Jesus.
The move contests the independence and evidentiary force of prominent attestations used to bridge later Christian belief back to a historical person.
Ehrman's reliance on multiple written and oral sources as attestations supporting a historical Jesus.
Price says Pliny and Tacitus likely learned Christian claims from Christians and argues that widespread oral traditions likewise establish belief and transmission, not the underlying event.
The Testimonium Flavianum is better explained as a Christian interpolation than as an authentic, pared-down notice written by Josephus.
Josephus is a major proposed non-Christian witness, so denying the passage's authenticity removes an important independent textual basis for Jesus's existence.
Ehrman's view that removing obvious Christian additions leaves an authentic and innocuous Josephan reference to Jesus.

Price argues that a reduced notice lacks a reason for Josephus to mention Jesus, cites linguistic and contextual interpolation arguments, associates the passage with Eusebius, and rejects selective redaction as evidence.
Hypothetical pre-Gospel sources and disputed extracanonical dependencies cannot securely bridge the canonical Gospels to a historical Jesus.
The argument targets the claimed multiplicity and independence of sources, a principal method for moving from extant Gospel texts toward historical conclusions.
Ehrman's appeal to multiple pre-Gospel written or oral sources and extracanonical Gospels as independent early witnesses.
Price treats Q, M, and L as theoretical constructs, questions Luke's asserted predecessors and eyewitness guarantees, and notes that dependence of extracanonical texts remains disputed.
Paul's archons language is most coherently read as describing a celestial Christ slain by demonic powers before later historicization.
This supplies a positive mythicist account of Christianity's earliest Christology rather than merely disputing particular evidence for a historical preacher.
Ehrman's reading of the Pauline epistles as evidence that Paul knew of a recently crucified historical Jesus.
Price notes Paul's failure to identify earthly executioners, interprets the rulers of the age as heavenly powers, and sketches a Gnostic salvation myth later transformed into incarnational history.
Paul's purported quotations of Jesus may be private revelations from an ascended Christ, while Paul's broader silence suggests Gospel sayings did not yet exist.
The argument challenges Pauline evidence for remembered earthly teaching and converts the epistles' sparse biographical content into support for developmental mythicism.
Ehrman's assertion that Paul refers on several occasions to teachings delivered by the historical Jesus.
Price reads the marriage command and Eucharistic words as possible revelations, invokes Paul's claim to receive his gospel through revelation, and argues absent traditions likely had not arisen.
Proposed interpolations in historicizing Pauline passages are not merely mythicist special pleading but have substantial non-mythicist scholarly precedents.
The move defends the legitimacy of removing passages often used as Pauline evidence for a recent Jesus, preserving a key supporting route for Price's case.
Ehrman's claim that mythicists invoke Pauline interpolations because they have a vested interest in eliminating contrary passages.
Price cites non-mythicist interpolation proposals concerning Galatians and First Corinthians to argue that each textual suggestion must be judged on its reasoning rather than the proponent's camp.
Trypho and Celsus accepted Jesus's birth, baptism, and crucifixion while disputing Christian supernatural interpretations of those events.
This rebuts Price's claimed ancient precedents for mythicism by distinguishing rejection of Christian theology from denial that Jesus existed or underwent earthly events.
Price's claim that Trypho and Celsus expressed something resembling an ancient mythicist view of Jesus.
Ehrman urges examination of the available texts and argues that both critics treat Jesus as born, baptized, tempted, and crucified while attacking Christian interpretations rather than his existence.
Historical Jesus research evaluates each tradition critically and can recover substantial claims without simply deleting miracles from Gospel stories.
The response rejects Price's characterization of historicist methodology and maintains that a non-miraculous historical reconstruction need not be an arbitrary residue of miracle tales.
Price's argument that removing spectacular elements leaves only banal stories and amounts to discredited rationalistic demythologizing.
Ehrman says much can be inferred without conceding any miracle, distinguishes modern critical evaluation from nineteenth-century naturalizing explanations, and calls Price's target a straw man.
Extant Gnostic writings are too late to establish a Gnostic background for Paul's letters from the 50s.
The chronology directly challenges the textual foundation for interpreting Paul's crucified Jesus as a celestial Gnostic figure rather than a historical person.
Price's claim that Gnostic myths predated Christianity and developed from older Jewish traditions.
After disputing a celestial reading of Paul's rulers, the exchange turns to whether Gnosticism existed early enough to supply Paul's conceptual background.
Jesus probably received no individual burial, and the Joseph of Arimathea tomb account arose later to support an empty-tomb tradition.
The argument shows that rejecting a major Gospel burial narrative does not require rejecting Jesus's existence and illustrates Ehrman's historical method.
Price's question about why Ehrman abandoned his former acceptance of Joseph's tomb and the women's empty-tomb visit.
During Price's questioning period, Ehrman explains how comparative evidence about Roman crucifixion practices altered his assessment of the burial story.
Belief in Jesus's resurrection was the indispensable catalyst that transformed attachment to a Jewish teacher into Christianity.
It supplies a historical causal model for Christianity's emergence from followers of a recently crucified person without affirming that a resurrection occurred.
Price's presentation of Burton Mack's view that diverse Jesus communities, rather than resurrection belief, began Christianity.
The speakers consider whether resurrection experiences were Christianity's starting point or merely one motif among several early Jesus communities.
The sources overwhelmingly describe a Galilean man acting on earth and provide no corresponding narratives about a divine Joshua acting in heaven.
This is a direct comparative-probability argument that the surviving source pattern is more expected if Christianity began with an earthly Jesus.
Price's mythicist model in which the original Jesus was a celestial deity rather than a Galilean human being.
After establishing their shared concern with historical probability, Ehrman asks which hypothesis better explains the kinds of Jesus traditions actually preserved.
Jesus may derive from an older Israelite theophany in which Yahweh appeared as a subordinate divine son distinguished from the Most High God.
The proposal furnishes a positive mythic and scriptural genealogy for a divine Jesus figure, rather than relying solely on doubts about Gospel historicity.
Ehrman's argument that the sources contain earthly Jesus stories but no stories about a divine Joshua living in heaven.
Price responds to the contrast between terrestrial narratives and a celestial Jesus by locating Christology in survivals of pre-monotheistic Israelite religion.
A Jewish man crucified by Romans is intrinsically more probable than a heavenly Jesus crucified by demons because Roman crucifixions are abundantly attested.
The argument directly compares the rival existence hypotheses using background knowledge and claims a strong prior-probability advantage for an earthly Jesus.
Price's proposal that the originating Jesus was a divine or celestial being derived from ancient theophanic traditions.
Ehrman redirects the discussion from theophanies to the historically documented Roman practice of crucifying Jews in first-century Palestine.
An ordinary crucified teacher would not adequately explain the emergence of Christianity; the causally effective figure is the mythic miracle-working Christ.
It attacks the explanatory sufficiency of a minimal historical Jesus and argues that conceding an ordinary victim does not account for the movement's origin.
Ehrman's contention that commonplace Roman crucifixion makes an earthly crucified Jew the more probable origin of Jesus belief.
The exchange distinguishes the richly mythologized Gospel character from a hypothetical ordinary person who might remain after supernatural features are removed.
Jesus's baptism by John is more probable than derivation from a Zoroastrian initiation story because John and his Jewish baptizing activity are independently attested.
The example demonstrates Ehrman's broader method of identifying plausible historical kernels and challenges mythicist dependence on remote literary parallels.
Price's treatment of Gospel episodes as literary constructions rather than memories involving a historical Jesus.
Ehrman contrasts a locally plausible event involving the attested John the Baptist with Price's proposed Zoroastrian source for Mark's baptism narrative.
Historical reconstructions of Jesus remain speculative paradigms imposed on fragmentary evidence, as shown by persistent disagreement over who a historical Jesus was.
The claim limits the certainty available to historicism and supports treating mythicism as one competing explanatory model rather than a demonstrably excluded position.
Ehrman's repeated probability arguments that ordinary historical explanations fit the early Christian evidence better than mythic parallels.
Price steps back from individual parallels to characterize historical inquiry as a hermeneutical process of testing rival organizing models against incomplete data.
Gnosticism and Zoroastrianism are poor paradigms for the earliest Jesus traditions because the relevant authors show no such knowledge and Gnostic evidence is later and Christian-influenced.
The synthesis challenges two principal comparative frameworks used for mythicism and replaces them with chronologically and culturally nearer explanations of the sources.
Price's claim that historians construct speculative paradigms and that his mythicist framework can organize the evidence plausibly.
After agreeing that historians test explanatory paradigms, Ehrman argues that the proposed Persian and Gnostic models lack the necessary early evidentiary footing.
The historically reconstructable Jesus cannot be securely known, and a personalized savior may displace the only possible historical standard.
The claim directly limits what historical inquiry can recover and explains how remembered or personalized religious figures can eclipse any historical person.
The questioner's comparison of Ehrman's remembered Jesus with Price's mythologized or personalized Jesus.
Asked whether misremembering and creating a personal Jesus both make the Gospel figure fictional, Price argues that the personalized savior subsumes an uncertain historical reconstruction.
Miraculous Gospel stories can be rejected without denying that Jesus existed, just as false divine claims about Augustus do not erase Augustus.
This directly supports the historical-Jesus side by separating legendary accretions from the underlying person's existence and historical recoverability.
Price's argument that an unknowable historical Jesus is subsumed by an imaginary or personalized savior.
Ehrman agrees that miracle traditions are unhistorical but argues that their falsity does not negate Jesus's existence and that substantial historical claims remain recoverable.
Galatians 1:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 are textually secure, and rejecting them as interpolations merely because they conflict with mythicism is methodologically unsound.
These Pauline passages are presented as early evidence for Jesus and his relations, so their textual authenticity bears directly on the debate's central evidence.
Price's earlier assertion that key Pauline references to Jesus and James may be interpolations or textual variants.
Responding to a request for interaction with Price's interpolation claim, Ehrman cites unanimous manuscript inclusion, Pauline style, theology, and scholarly textual methods.
Early patristic evidence and the absence of manuscripts from the relevant period leave genuine uncertainty about whether disputed Pauline passages were interpolated.
The move defends the possibility that crucial Pauline evidence for a historical Jesus entered the text later, preserving a core mythicist challenge.
Ehrman's claim that the Pauline passages are textually secure and that interpolation arguments are scholarship by convenience.
Price replies that non-mythicist scholars raised the proposals, invokes patristic textual evidence, and argues that missing early manuscripts preclude confident denial of interpolation.
Paul regarded Jesus as a preexistent divine being who became an actual human, born of a woman and a Jew, with disciples and brothers.
The proposition directly uses Paul's early testimony to argue that exalted or angelic Christology still presupposed a historical human Jesus.
The questioner's suggestion that Paul's preexistent angelic Christ might place Jesus outside the Gospel-era human setting.
Asked whether Ehrman's reading of Paul as describing a great angel supports an earlier nonhuman Christ, Ehrman distinguishes preexistence from the subsequent human life.
An ordinary itinerant teacher or exorcist would be too commonplace to explain the exalted Christ myth, much as a mere strongman would not adequately explain Hercules.
This is a direct mythicist argument that positing a mundane historical nucleus does not adequately account for the scale and character of the resulting mythology.
The questioner's proposal that myths could accumulate around a relatively charismatic historical person, as stories did around Elvis.
Price compares a proposed ordinary Jesus with commonplace healers and modern religious celebrities, arguing that such a figure is inadequate as the foundation of the Christ myth.
Jesus has substantially stronger and earlier evidence than Hercules, Krishna, or Moses, including multiple Gospels and Pauline Christ traditions from the first century.
The comparative quality and proximity of the sources are a principal affirmative reason for treating Jesus as historical rather than analogous to legendary figures.
Price's comparison of Jesus with Hercules, Aesop, Krishna, and Moses and his claim that a mundane nucleus is inadequate.
Ehrman counters that the relevant legendary figures lack the kind of early Gospel and Pauline evidence available for Jesus, even under the assumption of mythicism.
Christianity cannot be explained as a natural evolution of existing Jewish ideas because its earliest attestation centers on a crucified Messiah, while much contrary material is centuries too late.
The argument rejects a proposed scriptural and Jewish-development origin for Christianity while defending the chronological priority of first-century historical evidence.
The questioner's proposal that Christianity naturally developed from preexisting Jewish texts, angelology, and stories of an earlier Jesus.
Ehrman argues that a crucified Messiah was not supplied by ordinary Jewish development and that second- through fourth-century reports cannot establish beliefs in the 20s.

Unlike securely embedded rulers such as Augustus, Jesus is historically free-floating because his narrative links to Herod, Pilate, Caiaphas, and the Sanhedrin are literarily or historically defective.
This supplies a direct criterion for mythicism: removing disputed narrative anchors leaves Jesus insufficiently woven into independently explicable history.
Ehrman's claim that comparing Jesus with Moroni is inapt because Paul and the Gospels present Jesus as a human being.
Price says Moroni was presented as an ancient historical figure, then argues that Jesus differs from Augustus because Gospel synchronisms can be removed on historical and literary grounds.
Historical existence is established probabilistically by comparing independent, proximate sources, and Jesus has materially better evidence than figures known only from late singular hearsay.
The move states the affirmative side's governing historical method and explains why the surviving source pattern supports Jesus despite dependence on transmitted reports.
The questioner's charge that Ehrman's case rests entirely on hearsay no better than claims concerning Noah or Abraham.
Ehrman explains that historians assess probabilities through source independence, proximity, agreement, and critical examination rather than demanding repeatable scientific certainty about the past.
Early Christians would not have invented a crucified Messiah because Jewish expectations portrayed the Messiah as God's victorious anointed ruler, not someone destined for crucifixion.
This directly defends a major historical-existence argument: the tradition's clash with prior messianic expectations is offered as evidence against fabrication.
The questioner's claim that inventors could conveniently eliminate an ordinary fictional Jesus by having the Romans crucify him.
An audience member challenges Ehrman's appeal to crucifixion as unlikely invention, proposing that killing Jesus conveniently prevented exposure of an unimpressive or ordinary figure.

Paul's existence and authorship of seven coherent letters are historically well supported by independent early references, pseudonymous Pauline writings, and consistent linguistic, theological, and situational evidence.
Paul and the letters judged authentic are foundational early sources for Ehrman's historical case, so defending their provenance supports his evidence for Jesus.
The audience question suggesting that Paul or the writings attributed to him might merely be characters and events in somebody's story.
The final audience question challenges whether historians can establish that Paul existed and that writings attributed to him came from a real person describing real people and events.

The Pauline epistles need not come from a single historical Paul because the corpus shows pseudepigraphy, anachronisms, contradictions, and multiple authorship comparable to the writings falsely attributed to Peter.
This attacks the authenticity and unity of the Pauline evidence that Ehrman treats as an early source, weakening a major pillar of the historical-Jesus case.
Ehrman's argument that external references, multiple Pauline imitators, and seven internally coherent letters provide substantial evidence for Paul and authentic authorship.
Ehrman has just defended Paul through Acts, First Clement, multiple pseudonymous authors who presupposed him, and seven letters said to cohere in language, theology, and historical setting.
